# How to Turn a Meeting into a Clear, Shareable Summary Using AI

Most of us have been there. You leave a meeting with your head full of ideas, decisions, and deadlines — but your notes look like a toddler's doodle. What if you could skip the frantic scribbling and get a clean, ready-to-share summary in minutes?

You can. This guide walks you through the process step by step.

**What you need before you start:** A device to record or stream your meeting (phone, tablet, or computer), an internet connection, and a free account with at least one transcription tool (Otter.ai has a free tier). No paid plans required.

---

## Step 1 — Enable live transcription during your meeting

The goal here is to capture every word as it's spoken, so nothing gets lost.

Before your call starts, open your meeting tool and look for the option to turn on captions or transcription. In **Zoom**, you'll find this under the live transcript button in the toolbar at the bottom of your call screen — click it and select "Start Transcript." In **Microsoft Teams**, look for the three-dot menu during a call and choose "Turn on live captions." In **Google Meet**, click the closed-caption button in the toolbar at the bottom of the screen.

If you're using **Otter.ai**, start a new conversation in the app and tap the record button before your meeting begins. Share the meeting link so attendees can join.

You'll see words appearing on your screen in real time as people speak.

💬 **Example prompt you can use right now:**

> "Summarise this meeting transcript in bullet points. Include key decisions, action items with owners, and any deadlines. Keep the summary under 150 words."

You'll know it worked when you see a full transcript appearing on screen as the meeting progresses, with each speaker's words captured in order.

---

## Step 2 — Record the call if you forgot to enable transcription

Sometimes you forget to set up transcription in advance. That's fine — you can still capture everything.

If you're on a phone call or an in-person meeting, open your phone's voice recorder app and hit record. Most phones store these recordings in the voice memos or voice recorder app. If you're using a desktop, tools like **Descript** (descript.com) can record your screen and audio directly — just download the free app, click "New Recording," and choose audio-only if you just need sound.

For in-person meetings, position your phone on the table facing the group. If people are speaking from different directions, a Bluetooth speaker can help amplify voices clearly.

💬 **Example recording setup:**

> "New Recording → Audio Only → [Meeting name: 'Team standup 5 June'] → Record"

You'll know it worked when you see a waveform or timer running on your screen, confirming audio is being captured.

---

## Step 3 — Convert your recording to text using a transcription tool

Now you need to turn your audio into written text. This is called transcription — essentially the AI listens to the recording and writes down every word.

If you used **Otter.ai**, your transcript is already done. Open the conversation in the app and you'll see the full text ready to copy. Tap the three dots on any section to copy the whole thing.

If you recorded with your phone or another tool, upload the audio file to **Descript** by clicking "Import" and selecting your file. Descript will process the audio and show you the transcript alongside a playhead so you can click any word to jump to that moment in the recording.

**Google's Recorder app** (available on Pixel phones) also transcribes offline — open the app, play your recording, and tap "Transcribe" to generate text without needing the internet.

💬 **Example action:**

> "Open Otter.ai → select your meeting → tap 'Share' → tap 'Copy transcript'"

You'll know it worked when you have a block of text on your screen that reads like a written conversation, with speaker labels and timestamps.

---

## Step 4 — Feed the transcript to an AI summariser

Here's where the magic happens. You paste your transcript into a conversational AI (a chatbot that understands context) and ask it to create a summary.

Open **ChatGPT** (chatgpt.com), **Claude** (claude.ai), or **Google Gemini** (gemini.google.com). Create a new conversation, paste the full transcript into the message box, and send a summary request — this is called a prompt.

A prompt is simply the instruction you give the AI. The clearer it is, the better your output.

💬 **Example prompt to copy:**

> "Summarise this meeting transcript in bullet points. Include key decisions, action items with owners, and any deadlines. Keep the summary under 150 words."

> "Turn this transcript into a meeting summary with three sections: What was discussed, What was decided, and What needs to happen next."

You can adjust the length or format based on your needs. If you need owners for each action item, say so explicitly.

You'll know it worked when the AI returns a clean, structured list of the most important points from your meeting.

---

## Step 5 — Polish and share your summary

AI summaries are usually solid, but a quick human review catches any mistakes and adds missing context.

Read through the summary and check these three things:

- **Names** — AI can mix up "Emma" and "Emily" if they sound similar
- **Dates and deadlines** — double-check that dates match what was actually said
- **Action items** — make sure each task has a name attached so it's clear who's doing what

Add a sentence or two in your own words if something important was implied rather than said directly.

Format it simply: bold headings for sections (like "Decisions" or "Actions"), bullet points for each item. This makes it easy for anyone to scan.

Then share it — paste it into an email, a Slack message, or your team's shared notes folder.

💬 **Example share text:**

> "Hi team — here's a summary from today's catch-up. Actions are listed at the bottom. Let me know if I've missed anything!"

You'll know it worked when a colleague replies confirming they read it or adds a small correction, showing the summary landed clearly.

---

## Common mistakes

### Mistake 1: Using low-quality audio
**The problem:** Background noise, distant microphones, or multiple people talking over each other makes transcription less accurate.
**The fix:** Use a headset or noise-cancelling microphone. For in-person meetings, place your recording device in the centre of the table. In virtual calls, remind participants to mute when not speaking.

### Mistake 2: Pasting a transcript without a clear prompt
**The problem:** Throwing raw text at an AI without instructions often gives you a generic wall of text that doesn't highlight decisions or actions.
**The fix:** Always include a specific prompt that tells the AI what format you want and what to prioritise (see the examples in Step 4 above).

### Mistake 3: Skipping the human review
**The problem:** AI occasionally mishears words, especially names or technical terms, which can lead to embarrassing errors in shared summaries.
**The fix:** Spend 60 seconds scanning for names, dates, and action items before sending. A quick read-through catches almost all errors.

---

## What this means for you

- **In everyday life:** Use this process for family discussions, study groups, community meetings, or medical appointments where you want a reliable record. You can capture information without scrambling to write everything down by hand.

- **At work or in business:** Turn every team sync, client call, or project kickoff into a tidy recap that goes straight to email or your team's shared folder. This saves hours of typing up notes afterwards and cuts down on "I missed that" messages from colleagues.

- **If you're just getting started:** Pick one upcoming meeting, enable live transcription (Step 1), and run the resulting text through an AI summariser (Steps 3–4). You don't need to do the whole process perfectly the first time — just try it once and you'll immediately see how much mental load it removes.
